items.title: Washington Is Taking Control of AI
items.summary_html:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia is becoming a turning point in Washington’s battle over AI and China. NLW examines how the fallout is empowering China hawks, accelerating chip export restrictions, and raising questions that go well beyond the disputed spy allegations. Plus, the competing arguments over selling chips to China—and what new leadership at Nvidia could mean for the financing that keeps the AI boom moving.

items.title: Navigating the Maze of Production Machine Learning - Miguel Otero Pedrido
items.summary: Miguel Otero Pedrido, ML AI Engineer at Zapier and founder of The Neural Maze, joins Alexey Grigorev to discuss building ML and AI systems for production. We discussed: When traditional ML still beats LLMs Solving the cold start problem with contextual bandits for recommenders Avoiding comprehension debt as ML shifts toward AI system design Trace redaction pipelines and error analysis on agent traces at Zapier Watch the original recording: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xC5lqvfSfLU Join DataTalks.Club: https://datatalks.club/slack.html
items.summary_html:
Miguel Otero Pedrido, ML AI Engineer at Zapier and founder of The Neural Maze, joins Alexey Grigorev to discuss building ML and AI systems for production. We discussed:

  • When traditional ML still beats LLMs
  • Solving the cold start problem with contextual bandits for recommenders
  • Avoiding comprehension debt as ML shifts toward AI system design
  • Trace redaction pipelines and error analysis on agent traces at Zapier

Watch the original recording: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xC5lqvfSfLU

Join DataTalks.Club: https://datatalks.club/slack.html

items.title: Implementing Federated Learning to enhance Agentic AI
items.summary: How can AI models learn from private data without compromising privacy? Chris is joined by Lorenzo Sani, Research Scientist at Flower Labs and PhD researcher at Cambridge, to explore federated learning and privacy-preserving AI. They discuss how collaborative learning can expand access to private data for LLM training, how model trajectories can help improve agentic AI systems, and the benefits of open-weight models. The conversation also explores real-world applications of locally hosted AI agents, from healthcare and robotics to everyday automation (for a Halloween party). items.title: The hidden costs of CREATE TEMP TABLE
items.summary: Tip: watch on YouTube. Since episode 193, the video shows charts and illustrations as we talk. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gAdhpYewLZ8 Nik and Kirk discuss the hidden costs of CREATE TEMP TABLE: dead tuples and catalog bloat, and the shared invalidation queue that every session has to read. They cover why thousands of idle sessions make it much worse, what it looks like in wait events, and what to use instead. Here are some links to things they mentioned: Times are podcast times of the first mention. Main link [00:34:15] Temp tables in the request path: where the cliff is, and what LWLock:SInvalWrite really tells you (DBLab Forge brief, PostgresAI) https://console.postgres.ai/shared/brief/dfe99713-f5a8-483b-9aab-1606a883b75d Michael [00:00:44] Michael's post about taking a few months off (X) https://x.com/michristofides/status/2117283823314674021 Episodes [00:06:12] UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 https://postgres.fm/episodes/uuidv4-vs-uuidv7 Postgres docs [00:01:32] CREATE TABLE, Compatibility: temporary tables vs the SQL standard's global temporary tables (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html#SQL-CREATETABLE-COMPATIBILITY [00:04:34] CREATE TABLE, TEMPORARY: autovacuum cannot vacuum or analyze temporary tables (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html#SQL-CREATETABLE-TEMPORARY [00:15:40] LWLock wait events, including SInvalWrite and SInvalRead (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/monitoring-stats.html#WAIT-EVENT-LWLOCK-TABLE [00:19:16] max_locks_per_transaction (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-locks.html#GUC-MAX-LOCKS-PER-TRANSACTION [00:27:14] CREATE TABLE, ON COMMIT: PRESERVE ROWS, DELETE ROWS, DROP (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html#SQL-CREATETABLE-PARMS-ON-COMMIT [00:32:24] CREATE TABLE, UNLOGGED (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html#SQL-CREATETABLE-UNLOGGED [00:37:45] DISCARD (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-discard.html Postgres source and history [00:18:11] sinvaladt.c: MAXNUMMESSAGES, the 4,096-message invalidation queue https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/3d342deeb433060dbea02fdd276656a5563275d5/src/backend/storage/ipc/sinvaladt.c [00:18:49] Increase the number of fast-path lock slots (Tomas Vondra, 2024, Postgres 18) https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/c4d5cb71d229095a39fda1121a75ee40e6069a2a [00:23:38] Postgres 14 release notes: better scalability with many connections (Andres Freund's work) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/14.0/ [00:35:43] Rewrite the sinval messaging mechanism to reduce contention (Tom Lane, 2008) https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/fad153ec45299bd4d4f29dec8d9e04e2f1c08148 Tools [00:13:10] pg_repack https://github.com/reorg/pg_repack [00:20:24] PgBouncer, server_reset_query (default DISCARD ALL) https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html#server_reset_query [00:24:06] Amazon RDS Performance Insights https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PerfInsights.html [00:24:12] pg_ash, active session history for Postgres https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash Other [00:24:39] Linux Performance Tools, talk (Brendan Gregg) https://youtu.be/FJW8nGV4jxY [00:36:41] Don't Do This: Don't create temporary tables in frequently executed code (PostgreSQL wiki) https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This#Don.27t_create_temporary_tables_in_frequently_executed_code Corrections (checked against the Postgres source after recording) [00:13:58] Two temp tables and an index are not "three records in, three out". Each temp table adds at least 13 catalog rows (pg_class, pg_type, pg_attribute, pg_depend), about 31 if it has a text column, and the index adds more. So 10M queries a day means at least 600 million catalog row changes, not 60M. [00:15:47] sinval means shared invalidation (of the catalog and relation caches), not "snapshot invalidation". [00:18:49] LWLock:LockManager: up to Postgres 17 a session has 16 fast-path lock slots; Postgres 18 has 64 by default and scales them with max_locks_per_transaction. But temp-table DDL takes AccessExclusiveLock, which never uses the fast path, so raising the setting does not make this wait go away (the brief measured 6.6 to 12.7% LockManager with it set to 1024). [00:25:09] The invalidation queue is a circular buffer of 4,096 messages, but writers never wait for readers. When it is half full (2,048 messages), the session that is furthest behind gets a catch-up signal, and it passes the signal on, one session at a time. When it is full, sessions that have not read are reset and must rebuild all their caches. Writers wait on SInvalWriteLock because there is one such lock for the whole cluster, and both a write (which flags every session) and a queue cleanup (which scans every session) hold it. [00:27:26] ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS does not make dead tuples: at commit it truncates the table and its indexes. And ON COMMIT DROP is not slow mostly because of more messages: without idle sessions the cost is catalog changes and file create and unlink; sinval is under 1%. Clarifications [00:04:02] Temp table data is invisible to other sessions, but the definition and statistics are visible (pg_class, pg_stat_all_tables). [00:05:32] The docs glossary defines bloat, and the definition includes dead row versions. [00:14:56] Wraparound: load is not the condition. Autovacuum never freezes temp tables, so any long-lived temp table holds back datfrozenxid. [00:17:05] "Catalog is global": the catalog is per database and ...

  • [00:04:34] CREATE TABLE, TEMPORARY: autovacuum cannot vacuum or analyze temporary tables (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html#SQL-CREATETABLE-TEMPORARY
  • [00:15:40] LWLock wait events, including SInvalWrite and SInvalRead (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/monitoring-stats.html#WAIT-EVENT-LWLOCK-TABLE
  • [00:19:16] max_locks_per_transaction (docs) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-locks.html#GUC-MAX-LOCKS-PER-TRANSACTION

Postgres source and history

  • [00:18:11] sinvaladt.c: MAXNUMMESSAGES, the 4,096-message invalidation queue https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/3d342deeb433060dbea02fdd276656a5563275d5/src/backend/storage/ipc/sinvaladt.c
  • [00:18:49] Increase the number of fast-path lock slots (Tomas Vondra, 2024, Postgres 18) https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/c4d5cb71d229095a39fda1121a75ee40e6069a2a
  • [00:23:38] Postgres 14 release notes: better scalability with many connections (Andres Freund's work) https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/14.0/
  • [00:35:43] Rewrite the sinval messaging mechanism to reduce contention (Tom Lane, 2008) https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/fad153ec45299bd4d4f29dec8d9e04e2f1c08148

  • [00:13:10] pg_repack https://github.com/reorg/pg_repack
  • [00:20:24] PgBouncer, server_reset_query (default DISCARD ALL) https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html#server_reset_query
  • [00:24:06] Amazon RDS Performance Insights https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PerfInsights.html
  • [00:24:12] pg_ash, active session history for Postgres https://github.com/NikolayS/pg_ash


Other

  • [00:24:39] Linux Performance Tools, talk (Brendan Gregg) https://youtu.be/FJW8nGV4jxY
  • [00:36:41] Don't Do This: Don't create temporary tables in frequently executed code (PostgreSQL wiki) https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This#Don.27t_create_temporary_tables_in_frequently_executed_code


Corrections (checked against the Postgres source after recording)

  • [00:13:58] Two temp tables and an index are not "three records in, three out". Each temp table adds at least 13 catalog rows (pg_class, pg_type, pg_attribute, pg_depend), about 31 if it has a text column, and the index adds more. So 10M queries a day means at least 600 million catalog row changes, not 60M.
  • [00:15:47] sinval means shared invalidation (of the catalog and relation caches), not "snapshot invalidation".
  • [00:18:49] LWLock:LockManager: up to Postgres 17 a session has 16 fast-path lock slots; Postgres 18 has 64 by default and scales them with max_locks_per_transaction. But temp-table DDL takes AccessExclusiveLock, which never uses the fast path, so raising the setting does not make this wait go away (the brief measured 6.6 to 12.7% LockManager with it set to 1024).
  • [00:25:09] The invalidation queue is a circular buffer of 4,096 messages, but writers never wait for readers. When it is half full (2,048 messages), the session that is furthest behind gets a catch-up signal, and it passes the signal on, one session at a time. When it is full, sessions that have not read are reset and must rebuild all their caches. Writers wait on SInvalWriteLock because there is one such lock for the whole cluster, and both a write (which flags every session) and a queue cleanup (which scans every session) hold it.
  • [00:27:26] ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS does not make dead tuples: at commit it truncates the table and its indexes. And ON COMMIT DROP is not slow mostly because of more messages: without idle sessions the cost is catalog changes and file create and unlink; sinval is under 1%.

Clarifications

  • [00:04:02] Temp table data is invisible to other sessions, but the definition and statistics are visible (pg_class, pg_stat_all_tables).
  • [00:05:32] The docs glossary defines bloat, and the definition includes dead row versions.
  • [00:14:56] Wraparound: load is not the condition. Autovacuum never freezes temp tables, so any long-lived temp table holds back datfrozenxid.
  • [00:17:05] "Catalog is global": the catalog is per database and ...

items.title: Why Enterprise AI Isn't Delivering ROI | Ahmed Bashir, DevRev
items.summary: The pattern is familiar to every enterprise leader: the AI demo works perfectly, the enterprise deployment disappoints, and the CIO can't explain why. Ahmed Bashir, Chief Technology Officer of DevRev, joins Craig Smith with a specific and well-supported answer: the problem isn't the model. It's that enterprise data is organizationally complex, fragmented across dozens of tools, locked behind conditional permissions, organized by custom schemas, and every prominent AI benchmark tests models against flat files with pre-packaged data, which has nothing to do with how enterprise data actually lives. DevRev's Enterprise Bench is the first benchmark to test complete agent harnesses against a realistically distributed enterprise environment where the agent must find, relate, and validate information before performing any task, and the results expose a gap that pre-packaged benchmarks hide entirely. The most striking finding: DevRev's system achieves 50% higher accuracy than Claude Code using the identical Opus family model. The entire delta comes from the shared memory layer, the governance, semantic understanding, and orchestration that sits between the model and the enterprise data. Ahmed's analogy is precise: upgrading a CPU cannot compensate for insufficient RAM, because they perform fundamentally different functions. A more powerful model cannot make up for a weak memory layer for the same reason. The conversation also covers why Enterprise Bench aspires to be for AI agents what TPC benchmarks became for databases in the 1980s - the independent standard that ended vendor benchmark wars and gave buyers a genuinely apples-to-apples comparison - and why the build-vs-buy question in enterprise AI has a quantifiable answer for the first time, visible on a public leaderboard that puts DIY configurations directly alongside proprietary systems. items.title: Interview #103 Somya Kapoor, CEO of IFS Loops
items.summary: Somya Kapoor, CEO of IFS Loops, breaks down why most AI agent projects fail on change management rather than technology, and why a company that waits for perfect data will never get an agent deployed. She explains why building an agent is now easy enough for an 11-year-old while getting one into production is not, how an agent that starts at 40-50% accuracy can reach 80-85% in weeks with a human handling the exceptions, and why we demand perfection from machines when people are only about 70% productive at their jobs. Somya also dives into why every digital worker needs a supervisor agent keeping an audit trail, and who answers when an agent misprocesses a purchase order at 3 AM. Finally, she shares which jobs agents will take and which new ones they create, and why regulation, not technology, will keep a human signing off in industries where one outage can leave millions without power. items.title: Interview #102 Alex Salazar, Co-founder & CEO at Arcade.dev
items.summary: Alex Salazar, Co-founder & CEO at Arcade.dev, breaks down why treating AI agents as teammates is an architectural dead end, and why they should be treated as software that is unpredictable enough to count as adversarial. He explains why security is usually the first team to say no, why an agent's own permissions are only half the problem when an intern could ask it for the CEO's pay, and what has to be true before a bank lets an agent wire money, from payee accounts registered ahead of time to checking the CRM so a refund is not hallucinated. Alex also dives into approval fatigue, research showing people check an agent's work less when they see it as a peer, and why no model should ever be trusted, open-weight or not. Finally, he shares why the vendors behind most agent strategies likely did not exist before 2024, and why agents moving money will feel mundane by the end of next year. items.title: Why Stripe Cut 500,000 Internal Docs Down to 5,000?
items.summary: What happens when AI agents start relying on the same messy docs your team already struggles to search? Demetrios hops into a Waymo in San Francisco with Dave Nunez , founder and CEO of Falconer and co-author of Documentation for Developers. They talk about why developers and agents need different things from docs, why agents sometimes skip up-to-date instructions, and how a stale internal document can contribute to a production incident. Dave shares how Stripe cut roughly 500,000 internal docs down to 5,000 worth maintaining. The conversation also covers how to capture the reasoning behind engineering decisions, when a diagram beats a wall of text, and who owns the fallout when an agent acts on bad information.
